sections.heading: 1.2 Phases and Classification of Matter

blocks.text: Matter is defined as anything that occupies space and has mass, and it is all around us. Solids and liquids are more obviously matter: We can see that they take up space, and their weight tells us that they have mass. Gases are also matter; if gases did not take up space, a balloon would not inflate (increase its volume) when filled with gas.

Solids, liquids, and gases are the three states of matter commonly found on earth (Figure 1.6). A solid is rigid and possesses a definite shape. A liquid flows and takes the shape of its container, except that it forms a flat or slightly curved upper surface when acted upon by gravity. (In zero gravity, liquids assume a spherical shape.) Both liquid and solid samples have volumes that are very nearly independent of pressure. A gas takes both the shape and volume of its container.

A fourth state of matter, plasma, occurs naturally in the interiors of stars. A plasma is a gaseous state of matter that contains appreciable numbers of electrically charged particles (Figure 1.7). The presence of these charged particles imparts unique properties to plasmas that justify their classification as a state of matter distinct from gases. In addition to stars, plasmas are found in some other high-temperature environments (both natural and man-made), such as lightning strikes, certain television screens, and specialized analytical instruments used to detect trace amounts of metals.

In a tiny cell in a plasma television, the plasma emits ultraviolet light, which in turn causes the display at that location to appear a specific color. The composite of these tiny dots of color makes up the image that you see. Watch this video to learn more about plasma and the places you encounter it.

Some samples of matter appear to have properties of solids, liquids, and/or gases at the same time. This can occur when the sample is composed of many small pieces. For example, we can pour sand as if it were a liquid because it is composed of many small grains of solid sand. Matter can also have properties of more than one state when it is a mixture, such as with clouds. Clouds appear to behave somewhat like gases, but they are actually mixtures of air (gas) and tiny particles of water (liquid or solid).

sections.heading: 1.2 Phases and Classification of Matter
sections.text: Matter is anything that occupies space and has mass. Matter is all around us. Solids and liquids are more obviously matter. We can see that they take up space. Their weight tells us that they have mass. Gases are also matter. A balloon inflates when filled with gas. Inflate means to increase its volume. If gases took no space, balloons would not inflate. Solids, liquids, and gases are the three states of matter. They are commonly found on earth (Figure 1.6). A solid is rigid. A solid possesses a definite shape. A liquid flows. It takes the shape of its container. A liquid forms a flat or slightly curved upper surface. This happens when acted upon by gravity. In zero gravity, liquids take a spherical shape. Solid and liquid volumes are nearly independent of pressure. A gas takes the shape of its container. A gas also takes the volume of its container. Plasma is a fourth state of matter. It occurs naturally in the interiors of stars. Plasma is a gaseous state of matter (Figure 1.7). It contains appreciable numbers of electrically charged particles. These charged particles give plasma unique properties. These properties separate plasma from gases as a distinct state. Plasmas are found in other high-temperature environments. These environments can be natural or man-made. Plasmas occur in lightning strikes. They are found in certain television screens. Special analytical instruments use plasma to detect trace amounts of metals. A plasma television has tiny cells. In each tiny cell, plasma emits ultraviolet light. This light makes that location display a specific color. These tiny dots of color make up the whole image. Watch this video to learn more about plasma. You can see the places where you encounter it. Some samples of matter have properties of solids, liquids, and/or gases. This can occur when the sample is composed of many small pieces. For example, we can pour sand as if it were a liquid. This is because it is composed of many small grains of solid sand. Matter can have properties of more than one state when it is a mixture. Clouds are an example of this. Clouds appear to behave somewhat like gases. In truth, clouds are mixtures. They mix air (gas) with tiny particles of water. These water particles are liquid or solid.

repaired_sections.heading: 1.2 Phases and Classification of Matter
repaired_sections.text: Matter is anything that takes up space and has mass. Matter is all around us. Solids and liquids are more obviously matter. Solids take up space. Liquids also take up space. Their weight tells us that they have mass. Gases are also matter. If gases did not take up space, a balloon would not inflate. Inflating means it increases its volume when filled with gas. Solids, liquids, and gases are three states of matter (Figure 1.6). They are commonly found on earth. A solid is rigid and has a definite shape. A liquid flows and takes the shape of its container. Under gravity, a liquid forms a flat or slightly curved top surface. In zero gravity, liquids take a spherical shape. Both liquid and solid samples have volumes that are almost independent of pressure. A gas takes both the shape and volume of its container. A fourth state of matter is plasma. Plasma occurs naturally in the interiors of stars. Plasma is a gaseous state of matter (Figure 1.7). It has many electrically charged particles. These charged particles give plasmas unique properties. These properties justify classifying plasma as a state of matter distinct from gases. Plasmas also exist in other high-temperature environments, both natural and man-made. They are found in lightning strikes and certain television screens. They are also used in specialized analytical instruments that detect trace amounts of metals. In a tiny cell in a plasma television, plasma emits ultraviolet light. This light causes the display at that spot to show a specific color. The mix of these tiny dots of color makes the image you see. Watch this video to learn more about plasma and the places you encounter it. Some samples seem to have properties of solids, liquids, or gases. They can show these properties at the same time. This can happen when a sample is made of many small pieces. For example, we can pour sand like a liquid. This is because sand consists of many small grains of solid sand. Matter can also have properties of more than one state as a mixture. Clouds are an example. Clouds seem to behave somewhat like gases. However, they are mixtures of air (gas) and tiny water particles. These water particles can be liquid or solid.
